FA 2 · Big Data Analytics · Live Apache Spark run

Watch Spark sort 100,000 real CERN collisions

Each collision at CERN's particle smasher leaves two "muons". From them we can work out the mass of the particle that made them. Press Run and watch the data get read, cleaned, sorted and counted. Particles appear as spikes in the charts below while it runs.

0 · The dataset: where it comes from

Real data, released to the public by CERN. Nothing here is simulated.
SourceCERN Open Data Portal
Recorded byCMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider
When2011 (data period Run2011A), 15 recording sessions
Collision energy7 TeV (two proton beams of 3.5 TeV)
Size100,000 collisions × 21 columns (14 MB CSV)
What was keptOnly collisions with two muons ("dimuon events")
LicenceCC0: free for anyone to use
Linkopendata.cern.ch/record/545
Run, Event which session / which collision type muon quality (G = global, T = tracker) E energy of the muon px, py, pz, pt its momentum (how hard it moves, and where) eta, phi direction: along / around the detector Q electric charge (+1 or −1) M mass of the parent particle (GeV): what we analyse

1 · How the data is taken and sorted

Every dot is a real collision moving through the Spark job. Colours show which group it gets sorted into.
J/ψ group (≈3.1 GeV)Υ group (≈9.5–10.4 GeV)Z group (≈91 GeV)everything elsefaulty row, removed
Now: press ▶ Run Spark job to start.
# 1 READ: load the collisions from storage
raw = spark.read.csv("dimuon.csv", schema=schema)# 2 CLEAN: recompute mass, drop faulty rows
df = raw.filter(abs(M_calc - M) / M <= 0.05).cache()# 3 MAP: each core labels its collisions
pairs = df.rdd.map(lambda e: (mass_slot(e.M), 1))# 4 SHUFFLE + REDUCE: same labels meet, add up
counts = pairs.reduceByKey(add)# 5 RESULTS: particles, sessions, detector map
counts.collect(); df.groupBy("Run").agg(...)
The highlighted line is the step the dots are in right now.

2 · Live event display: each collision as the detector sees it

While Spark runs, every processed collision is drawn here from its real numbers. Left: looking down the beam pipe (angle φ). Right: from the side (angle η). The two muon tracks curve in opposite directions because they have opposite charges.

Particles per 1,000 collisions in each recording session of 2011. The mix changes: the detector's save filter was re-tuned.

6 · Where muons hit the detector

Advanced · heatmap
The can-shaped detector cut open and laid flat. Darker = more hits. Even all around = no blind spots.

Line chart
The J/ψ spike seen from different parts of the detector. Narrower = sharper measurement.

What the run found

–particles discovered (5σ+), plus a strong hint
–faulty rows found and removed
0.55 %largest error in where a spike sits: the detector's scale is accurate
–more Z bosons per 1,000 collisions by the end of 2011
–sharper measurements in the detector's middle than its ends
~1.5×more data would push Υ(3S) past 5σ
